hints: Think about what actually pulls water up from the top of the plant, what happens in the leaf when water evaporates from mesophyll cells?
Recall the cohesion-tension theory: how do hydrogen bonds between water molecules, and between water and the xylem wall, help transmit that pull all the way down to the roots?
walkthrough:
**Start with the pull from the leaf**

Water is lost by transpiration from the leaves. This removes water from the xylem in the leaf and lowers the hydrostatic pressure there.

That creates tension, a pulling force, that draws water up from below. So statement 3 is true.

**See how the pull is transmitted**

Water molecules stick strongly to each other by hydrogen bonding. This is cohesion.

It means when the top molecules are pulled up, the whole column is pulled up together without breaking. So statement 1 is true.

**Check the help from the walls**

Water molecules also form hydrogen bonds with the cellulose in the xylem vessel walls. This is adhesion.

It helps the water column stick to the sides and resist gravity, keeping the continuous column moving upward. So statement 2 is true.

**Put it together**

All three statements describe parts of the cohesion-tension mechanism for upward movement in xylem.

That gives 1, 2 and 3, which is option A.

options.A: Correct. Cohesion, adhesion and the reduced hydrostatic pressure (tension) from transpiration all work together to move water up the xylem.
options.B: Incomplete. It correctly includes cohesion and adhesion but wrongly leaves out statement 3, the transpiration pull that provides the driving force.
options.C: Incomplete. It correctly includes cohesion and tension but wrongly leaves out statement 2, adhesion to the walls also supports the column.
options.D: Incomplete. It correctly includes adhesion and tension but wrongly leaves out statement 1, cohesion is essential to pull the whole column as one.
